content.title: U.S. 10-Year Treasury Yield Jumps to Highest Level Since Early Sept
content.summary: The 10-year U.S. Treasury yield rose to 4.275% in early trade, the highest level since early September, according to Tradeweb data.  The rise comes amid U.S. President Trump's latest tariff threats on several European countries over his plan to acquire Greenland.  "If the dispute over Greenland continues to escalate, it is quite possible that EU investors will sell off U.S. government bonds," BlueBay's Kaspar Hense said in a note.

content.title: U.S. Treasury Yield Curve Is Steepening
content.summary: U.S. long-dated Treasury yields were rising, while short-end yields edged lower in early trade, causing the Treasury curve to steepen. The day's potential drivers for Treasury yields include industrial production and capacity utilization data for December, as well as Federal Reserve speakers Michelle Bowman and Philip Jefferson.

content.title: U.S. Treasury Yields Little Changed; Fed Speeches Ahead
content.summary: U.S. Treasury yields were little changed in early trade, with data, geopolitics, and monetary policy expectations remaining the key inputs. Thursday's potential drivers include weekly jobless claims, as well as speeches by Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta President Raphael Bostic and Federal Reserve Bank of Kansas City President Jeffrey Schmid.

content.title: U.S. Treasury Yields Edge Lower Ahead of Data, Potential Supreme Court Decision
content.summary: U.S. Treasury yields edged lower in early trade with a busy U.S. economic calendar ahead, including retail sales and PPI for November as well as existing home sales for December.  Wednesday may also see the Supreme Court decision on the legality of the Ieepa tariffs.  "Our basic assumption is for them to be struck down, and we think the market is generally of the same opinion," ING's Padhraic Garvey said in a note.

content.title: Treasury Yields Slip After Inflation Report
content.summary: Treasury yields edged lower after a cooler-than-expected December inflation reading. Though headline inflation matched economists' expectations, investors care more about so-called core prices, which exclude volatile food and energy categories.
